rows.grounds: predicate of good and bad deeds
refers back to the binding doubt

items.question: Can good or bad deeds still bind the liberated person?
premises: The Anantakārikā declares that good and bad deeds are binding.
Such binding might be suspected for this person as well.
That suspicion should not arise in this case.
items.inference: Even if deeds are generally binding, they do not bind the person described here.
uncertainties: The exact identity or source of 'Anantakārikā' is not specified in the verse.
items.plain_english: The Anantakārikā indeed declared that good and bad deeds are binding, and one might suspect that for this person too; but that should not be the case.

rows.grounds: restricts death to the memory-lost case

items.question: Does the word 'api' imply liberation can occur with unlost memory at death?
premises: The word 'api' may suggest the possibility of death with unlost memory.
Death is properly spoken of only for one whose memory is lost.
Even if memory existed before death, it has no relevance at that moment.
items.inference: The possibility of unlost memory does not affect the point that death itself is not the cause of liberation.
uncertainties: The exact scriptural phrase containing 'api' is not quoted in this verse.
items.plain_english: From the word 'api' one might think death with unlost memory is possible, but death belongs only to one whose memory is lost; even if memory was present before death, what does that matter?

items.question: What does the optative mood indicate about death and liberation?
premises: The optative mood expresses possibility rather than necessity.
The time-expression in the text functions in that sense of possibility.
That expression declares that death is not a cause of liberation.
items.inference: The grammatical form supports the view that death does not directly cause liberation.
uncertainties: The specific verbal form being analyzed is not explicitly quoted.
items.plain_english: The optative expresses possibility, and the time-expression used there declares that death is not a cause of liberation.

rows.grounds: reason the body no longer binds
explains why the body was problematic

items.question: Why is 'kaivalya' treated as a doubtful designation here?
premises: The term 'kaivalya' can be an object of doubt.
The body that produced duality has become removable and is destroyed.
With that destruction, sorrowlessness is established.
items.inference: Because duality-producing embodiment is destroyed, the liberated state is better described as sorrowlessness than as isolated kaivalya.
uncertainties: The precise nuance of 'yāpya' (removable, to be expelled, or to be transcended) is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: Calling it 'kaivalya' is open to doubt, because the body that gave rise to duality has been destroyed; therefore sorrowlessness remains.

items.question: Does connection with one's own body differentiate the living-liberated person?
premises: Connection with another body does not differentiate the liberated person.
The living-liberated person still has a connection with his own body.
The same non-differentiating principle applies to that own-body connection.
items.inference: For the living-liberated, even connection with one's own body does not create real differentiation.
items.plain_english: Just as connection with another body does not differentiate him, so too, even for the living-liberated, connection with his own body does not differentiate him.

items.question: Does embodiment or its absence make any real difference for one non-different from Śiva?
premises: The liberated person rejects identification with the universe-form.
The liberated person is non-different from Śiva.
Embodiment and absence of embodiment are both considered.
items.inference: For one non-different from Śiva, there is no essential distinction between having a body and not having a body.
items.plain_english: Therefore, for one who has rejected the universe-form and is non-different from Śiva, there is indeed no distinction whether in the body or even in its absence.

items.question: Why is the state of 'kevalatva' mentioned now despite non-difference?
premises: A suspicion persists due to prior impressions of difference.
The teaching now addresses that lingering suspicion.
The term 'kevalatva' may also be used from another standpoint.
items.inference: The mention of 'kevalatva' is provisional, responding to residual impressions or to a different frame of reference.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'another measure' (mātrāntara) is not fully specified.
items.plain_english: Even so, because the suspicion arising from prior impressions of difference persists, the state of being-only is now mentioned, or else it is spoken of from another standpoint.

items.question: How is the liberated person described in relation to things and in the Traiśirasa text?
premises: Things do not know him as divided from them.
He is not known by them as divided.
The revered Traiśirasa also describes a state beyond the sun-moon pair.
items.inference: Liberation is marked by non-division and is supported by the Traiśirasa description of a transcendent state.
uncertainties: The syntax of 'tānyenaṃ na vidurbhinnaṃ taiḥ' allows slight variation in emphasis.
items.plain_english: They do not know him as divided, and he is called liberated; this is also stated in the revered Traiśirasa, in the state devoid of the sun and moon pair.

items.question: What characterizes the transcendent state described in the Traiśirasa passage?
premises: The state abides where even the absence of disgust is broken through.
It is steady on all sides like a post.
It is free from all mishap and beyond means of knowledge and cognition.
items.inference: The cited state is one of radical steadiness and transcendence beyond ordinary evaluative and cognitive structures.
uncertainties: The compound 'jugupsābhāvabhaṅgasthe' is terse and can be read in more than one nuanced way.
items.plain_english: It is a state where even the absence of disgust is broken through, steady on all sides like a post, free from all mishap, and beyond means of knowledge and cognition.

items.question: What happens to the doer of action in that interval of awareness?
premises: In that interval of awareness, the doer of action is dissolved.
Even as doer, he remains unstained.
The analogy of pot and space illustrates what remains when the limiting form is gone.
items.inference: The doer dissolves in awareness without stain, like space remaining when a pot is broken.
uncertainties: The role of 'pradhānaṃ' in the list is compressed and may be read as part of the example series.
items.plain_english: In that interval of awareness the doer of action is dissolved and remains unstained; as with pot and space, even when the pot is destroyed, space remains.

items.question: What becomes of the self when the limiting form is gone?
premises: The self does not perish like the broken limiting form.
The self is of the nature of Śiva.
The knower stands independent and pervades all things.
items.inference: When limitation falls away, the self is revealed as Śiva-natured, independent, and all-pervading.
items.plain_english: The self would not perish in that way; it would be of the nature of Śiva. Established as independent, the knower would spread through all things.

items.question: How is the liberated knower's state characterized beyond ordinary categories?
premises: For that knower, neither being nor non-being applies.
Neither fixed configuration nor conceptual construction applies.
This inner teaching is also spoken by the guru in the Gītā.
items.inference: The knower's state transcends the usual oppositions and conceptual determinations, as confirmed by the Gītā.
uncertainties: The phrase 'antarāgūrya' is compressed and may reflect a textual or interpretive difficulty.
items.plain_english: For him there is neither being nor non-being, neither configuration nor conceptual construction; this inner teaching the guru also spoke in the Gītā.

items.question: What determines the state one attains at the moment of leaving the body?
premises: A person remembers some state at the end while abandoning the body.
One goes to that very state remembered at the end.
This occurs because one has always been imbued with that state.
items.inference: The final remembrance reflects long-standing inner conditioning and determines the state attained.
items.plain_english: Whatever state one remembers while leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, because one has always been imbued with that state.

items.question: What practice is enjoined, and what happens if one dies when sattva predominates?
premises: Because final attainment follows remembrance, constant remembrance is enjoined.
One should remember the divine and also perform one's duty.
If sattva is predominant at death, the departing one goes upward.
items.inference: Continuous remembrance shapes the final state, and predominance of sattva leads to an upward departure.
items.plain_english: Therefore remember me at all times and fight; and when sattva is increased, then, having dissolved, one goes upward.

items.question: What characterizes death when rajas and tamas predominate?
premises: One may dissolve gradually into rajas and tamas.
Such a person goes toward bewilderment in wombs shaped by karma.
The senses are then encompassed by delusion, labored breathing, and fatigue.
items.inference: Predominance of rajas and tamas at death leads to a confused and afflicted transition.
items.plain_english: Gradually dissolved in rajas and tamas, one goes to bewilderment in karmic wombs; there the senses are encompassed by delusion, labored breathing, and fatigue.

rows.grounds: introduces the true moment of abandonment

items.question: Is the described death experience the same as actually abandoning the body?
premises: The experiences described above occur in the body.
Those experiences are not the actual abandonment of the body.
The true abandonment is a single final breath-natured moment.
items.inference: Death experiences within the body must be distinguished from the precise moment of bodily abandonment.
items.plain_english: This and similar death experiences occur in the body, but they are not the actual abandoning of the body; that is only the single final breath-natured moment.

items.question: What precisely marks the moment of separation from the body?
premises: Immediately after a certain moment, the body becomes like wood or a wall.
That moment is a minute fraction of the time of abandoning the body.
That fraction is what actually causes separation from the body.
items.inference: The decisive event of death is an instantaneous separation after which the body is merely inert matter.
items.plain_english: Immediately after that moment the body becomes like wood or a wall; that minute fraction of the time of abandoning the body is what causes separation from the body.

items.question: What is remembered at the moment of separation from the body?
premises: At that moment one is free from the pleasures and pains of that body.
Whatever is remembered then arises from awakened prior impressions.
The remembrance occurs in that precise moment of separation.
items.inference: At separation, consciousness is shaped not by bodily feeling but by the awakening of prior impressions.
items.plain_english: For at that very moment, freed from that body's pleasures and pains and so on, one remembers whatever arises from the awakening of prior impressions.

rows.grounds: possible qualities of the attained form

items.question: Why does one assume a particular form at the moment of separation?
premises: The form assumed arises from causes such as unseen merit, repeated practice, and descent of power.
One approaches that very form which is remembered.
That form may be characterized by happiness, suffering, or delusion.
items.inference: The post-separation form is determined by a complex of karmic, habitual, and grace-related causes.
uncertainties: The relative weight of 'adṛṣṭa', 'abhyāsa', and 'śaktipāta' is not specified.
items.plain_english: Due to causes such as unseen merit, abundance of practice, and descent of power, one assumes that very form, whether happy, suffering, or deluded.

items.question: Why might one attain a state beyond pleasure and pain or of the nature of bliss?
premises: One may attain a form devoid of pleasure and pain.
One may alternatively attain a form of the nature of bliss.
The attained state corresponds to what is remembered in consciousness.
items.inference: Even higher or neutral states at separation are determined by what consciousness remembers.
items.plain_english: Or if one attains a state devoid of pleasure and pain, or one of the nature of bliss, why does one go to that? Because that is what this one remembers in consciousness.

items.question: How does the body arise as a manifestation grounded in consciousness?
premises: What shone forth previously and more strongly appears as this body.
That manifestation rests on the foundation of consciousness.
Consciousness establishes that prior foundation through functioning as identity.
items.inference: The body is a manifestation grounded in consciousness through an identity-forming act.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic flow between the two halves of the verse is compressed.
items.plain_english: What previously shone forth more strongly appears as this body, grounded in consciousness; for whatever was previously established by consciousness through identity-functioning became its foundation.

items.question: What is meant by absorption in sattva, rajas, tamas, or knowable forms?
premises: Absorption is spoken of in sattva, rajas, tamas, and in knowable forms like blue and yellow.
Consciousness previously imagined a particular form.
That same consciousness becomes absorbed in what it had thus established.
items.inference: Absorption in qualities or objects is consciousness resting in forms it has itself previously constituted.
items.plain_english: That very absorption is declared in sattva, rajas, tamas, and in knowable forms such as blue and yellow, because consciousness rests in a form it had previously imagined.

items.question: How does consciousness relate to what it takes as its support, including the body?
premises: Consciousness first establishes something as its support.
It thereby makes that support operative.
Even when the body is such a support, it is comparable to any merely established object like a wall.
items.inference: The body has no privileged status apart from being an object established by consciousness as its support.
items.plain_english: Having first established it, consciousness makes it a support; therefore, even when the body is merely something established, it is no different in principle from a wall.

rows.grounds: relation of other things to the body

items.question: What distinguishes the body from other supports established by consciousness?
premises: The body has a distinction: it functions as the prior support for all other things established.
Other things operate through identity with that bodily support.
Even though this is so, that dependence is not ordinarily recognized.
items.inference: The body is uniquely primary among supports, yet its foundational role usually remains unnoticed.
items.plain_english: The body has this distinction: it is the prior support for all else. Although other things function through identity with it, that is not recognized even when it is present.
